summary: Describes how some fields of DHCP messages should be used on IEEE 1394 (FireWire) networks, because its link-layer addressing differs from Ethernet. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC clarifies how DHCP clients and servers fill in message fields on IEEE 1394 networks. It avoids relying on the link address, which can change across bridges.

questions: how to configure firewire devices with dhcp
how does dhcp work over ieee 1394
what is the dhcp client identifier on 1394
why is chaddr ignored on ieee 1394
subtitle: How DHCP message fields are used on IEEE 1394 networks.

tldr.problem: IEEE 1394 uses link addressing differently from Ethernet, so some DHCP fields need different rules for interoperability.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets the hardware type and length, reserves the client hardware address field, and directs clients to use a client identifier.
tldr.outcome: These rules adapt DHCP message fields for IEEE 1394 links; the RFC notes that a client can falsify its EUI-64 identifier.

today: RFC 2855 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Link-Address Difference
sections.content:
IEEE 1394 uses a different link-layer addressing method from conventional IEEE 802 or Ethernet networks. On Ethernet, DHCP may use the client hardware address field to return a reply. A 1394 node ID is transient and may not remain consistent across a 1394 bridge.

The RFC therefore says not to put the 1394 node ID in the chaddr field. A client should request a broadcast reply when 1394 ARP is not yet possible.
sections.plainLanguage: The usual hardware-address field cannot reliably identify a 1394 device across bridges. The RFC gives DHCP a different way to identify the client.

sections.title: 1394 DHCP Field Rules
sections.content:
On IEEE 1394, htype MUST be 24 and hlen MUST be 0. The sender MUST set chaddr to zero, and recipients and relay agents MUST ignore it.

Clients MUST use the client identifier option. They SHOULD include the EUI-64 node-unique identifier, whose type value is 27. In DHCPDISCOVER and DHCPREQUEST, clients SHOULD set the BROADCAST flag and set ciaddr to zero when requesting broadcast replies; the RFC specifies exceptions for BOUND, RENEWING, and REBINDING states.
sections.plainLanguage: The client uses a separate identifier instead of the hardware-address field. It can ask the server to broadcast a reply when the 1394 address-resolution method is not available.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that DHCP provides no authentication or security mechanisms. It points to the DHCP specification for potential exposures.

A malicious client can falsify its EUI-64 identifier and appear to be another client.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can claim another device's EUI-64 identifier. DHCP itself does not verify that claim.
